entries.title: Introducing Reflection Beam: an open-weight model for agentic coding on AWS
entries.summary: Reflection AI's Beam is an open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon tasks. This post shows how to deploy Beam on AWS: start with an Amazon SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint, or use Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference with JumpStart, SGLang, or vLLM for Kubernetes-native control over distributed GPU infrastructure.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Introducing Reflection Beam: an open-weight model for agentic coding on AWS

Reflection AI introduced Beam, an open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon tasks such as maintaining code, using tools, interpreting results, and completing multi-step workflows. The open-weight release gives developers and researchers control over the runtime, deployment environment, and customization process.

In this post, we explain Reflection’s vision and show how you can deploy Beam on AWS. Start with an Amazon SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint for a fully managed path. When you need Kubernetes-native control over distributed GPU infrastructure, use Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference with JumpStart, SGLang, or vLLM. We also explain how Beam’s 501 billion total parameters shape checkpoint storage, weight memory, sharding, and parallelism, while its 23 billion active parameters influence per-token compute.

At launch, Beam is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio).

Reflection’s vision for open intelligence

Reflection’s mission is to make intelligence open and accessible to all through open model weights, published research, and open source software. Its full AI stack spans models, core software, production infrastructure, and applications. Beam brings this approach to developers building software engineering and agentic systems.

About Reflection Beam

Beam is a sparse mixture-of-experts model for resolving software issues, modifying code, calling tools, and acting on intermediate results. It has 501 billion total parameters and 23 billion active parameters, and Reflection reports an effective context length of 1 million tokens.

Reflection releases Beam’s weights through Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam 1.0 is available in BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoint variants. These formats provide different memory footprints and hardware compatibility. You can deploy the model with the AWS managed JumpStart container configuration or inspect and customize the model with SGLang or vLLM in your AWS environment.

Understand the deployment architecture

Choose the serving path that meets your control and scaling requirements.

  • Start with a SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint when you want an AWS managed model package, endpoint, and invocation API without operating Kubernetes.
  • Use JumpStart on HyperPod Inference when you want the AWS managed container and model configuration on a HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS).
  • Use SGLang or vLLM on HyperPod Inference when you need to control the serving image, runtime arguments, quantization, or distributed execution.
  • Size the deployment for checkpoint storage, weight memory, KV cache, context length, batching, runtime overhead, and the supported parallelism.
  • Define the expected concurrency and latency targets, then configure replicas, caching, routing, and autoscaling from measured workload behavior.

The JumpStart real-time path packages the model, container, and endpoint behind a managed deployment workflow. The HyperPod path exposes the cluster and serving runtime so that you can control distributed execution, caching, routing, and scaling.

The following diagram shows the components used by the HyperPod path. Beam can be sourced through SageMaker JumpStart, Hugging Face Hub, or an optional Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) mirror. The distributed workers use the AWS managed JumpStart container or a custom SGLang or vLLM runtime.

Prerequisites

You need:

  • An AWS account with permissions for your selected SageMaker deployment path and its supporting AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), networking, and storage resources.
  • Access to Beam through SageMaker JumpStart or one of the Beam 1.0 checkpoint repositories on Hugging Face.
  • Acceptance of the model terms, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), and Python 3.11 or later.
  • GPU quota and capacity for a supported Beam configuration.

Plan and obtain GPU capacity

Beam’s 501 billion total parameters require a multi-GPU deployment. BF16 has the largest weight-memory requirement, so plan a multi-node configuration with enough aggregate GPU memory for the weights and runtime overhead. For FP8, use 

ml.p5.48xlarge
with NVIDIA H100 GPUs or 
ml.p5e.48xlarge
and 
ml.p5en.48xlarge
with H200 GPUs. For NVFP4, use 
ml.p6-b200.48xlarge
with NVIDIA B200 GPUs. Confirm that the released checkpoint, runtime, and parallel layout support the selected instance type.
  • Calculate memory for weights, KV cache, and runtime overhead for one replica, then confirm the estimate with a load test.
  • Choose an AWS Region that supports the required accelerated instance.
  • Check the service quota and available capacity for the selected instance type. Use on-demand capacity when available, or use a SageMaker training plan as a short-term reservation for scheduled work.
  • Allow time for image transfer, weight download, shard loading, and runtime initialization.

Path 1: Get started with a SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint

Use a JumpStart real-time endpoint first when you want the shortest path from the model catalog to a managed HTTPS endpoint. The sample supports the BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 model IDs through one variant-aware command. Its README and Python file are the source of truth for supported instance types, request schema, deployment command, and cleanup command.

  • Clone the sample repository.
  • Enter the SageMaker JumpStart deployment sample directory.
  • Create and activate a Python virtual environment.
  • Install the sample dependency.
  • Run the bounded deployment, invocation, and cleanup lifecycle for FP8.

    The command deploys the FP8 endpoint, sends a short request, prints the response, and cleans up the endpoint. Use 

    bf16
     or 
    nvfp4
     to select another checkpoint variant; NVFP4 is the default when you omit 
    --variant
    . Use the Python functions in the README when you need to keep an endpoint running.

Path 2: Deploy with SageMaker HyperPod Inference

Use HyperPod Inference when you need Kubernetes-native control over distributed GPU infrastructure. You can use the AWS managed JumpStart container configuration or deploy Beam with SGLang or vLLM. The HyperPod Inference deployment sample README and its configuration files are the source of truth for released manifests, model and image identifiers, supported runtime versions, and commands.

Before you begin, configure 

kubectl
access to an EKS-orchestrated HyperPod cluster with the HyperPod Inference Operator and required add-ons. You also need the cluster virtual private cloud (VPC), subnets, security groups, access to the selected Beam and runtime artifacts, and local NVMe capacity if you enable model caching. Use an isolated Hugging Face access token if the selected repository requires authentication.

Deploy a pinned Beam revision from Hugging Face Hub for development and experimentation. For production deployments and model caching, copy the checkpoint to Amazon S3 or Amazon FSx. HyperPod model and image caching can preload weights onto node-local NVMe storage and pre-pull the serving image.

The HyperPod Inference Gateway provides an OpenAI-compatible interface and routes requests across replicas. HyperPod Inference also supports managed tiered KV caching and intelligent routing. These are among the Amazon SageMaker Inference capabilities introduced in 2026.

The next diagram expands the model preparation and runtime request flow. When model caching is enabled, the Inference Operator warms eligible nodes with the selected weights and serving image. At runtime, the Inference Gateway and Endpoint Picker can direct each request to a suitable JumpStart-managed, SGLang, or vLLM replica.

Prepare deployment artifacts

Use immutable inputs so that you can reproduce deployment and performance results.

  • Use the JumpStart model release recorded in the deployment sample.
  • Choose the BF16, FP8, or NVFP4 checkpoint for a custom runtime.
  • For a custom runtime, keep the public Beam commit SHA and image digest in the sample release configuration.
  • Mirror the released image into a private Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository only when your cluster cannot pull the upstream image or your organization requires an approved registry.
  • Keep tokens, generated secrets, private model IDs, registry credentials, and unpublished results out of the repository.

Choose a serving path

Start with SageMaker JumpStart unless your workload requires a specific inference runtime or configuration.

Serving pathUse it whenWhat you manage
SageMaker JumpStartYou want an AWS-managed container and model configuration with less runtime maintenance.Select the Beam model version, supported instance type, endpoint configuration, and scaling policy.
SGLang or vLLMYou need a specific inference runtime or configuration, such as custom runtime arguments, parsers, quantization, or parallelism.Pin the supported runtime image, model revision, parser configuration, and distributed execution settings.

Deploy with SageMaker JumpStart

SageMaker JumpStart reduces container integration work while HyperPod retains control over cluster capacity, scaling, and observability.

  • In SageMaker Studio, open the JumpStart model catalog.
  • Under All public models, choose Beam.
  • Choose SageMaker HyperPod as the deployment target.
  • Select the cluster and Kubernetes namespace.
  • Enter an endpoint name, and choose Deploy.
  • Confirm the deployment status before invoking the endpoint with the released JumpStart request schema.

For an infrastructure-as-code workflow, use the released JumpStart configuration in the HyperPod sample. You can inspect the reflection-beam-jumpstart.yaml manifest template before configuring the deployment.

  • Clone the sample repository, and enter the HyperPod Beam directory.
  • Create the local configuration files described in the README.
  • Validate the JumpStart configuration before changing the cluster.
  • Deploy the JumpStart configuration.

The helper renders and applies the released 

JumpStartModel
resource without writing populated release values to disk.

Deploy with SGLang or vLLM

Choose SGLang or vLLM when you need direct control over the serving runtime. Before configuring the deployment, inspect the reflection-beam-sglang.yaml manifest template or the reflection-beam-vllm.yaml manifest template. The sample README remains the source of truth for released values and commands.

  • Clone the sample repository.
  • Enter the HyperPod Beam directory.
  • Create the local configuration files described in the README.
  • Validate the selected configuration before changing the cluster.
  • Deploy Beam, and wait for a terminal deployment state.

    Replace 

    sglang
    with 
    vllm
    to use vLLM. The helper validates the selected settings, applies the rendered manifest without writing release values to disk, waits with a fixed timeout, and prints diagnostics if deployment fails.

Invoke Beam

Invoke JumpStart endpoints with the released model request schema. For SGLang or vLLM, use the bounded smoke test included in the HyperPod sample.

Invoke the deployed endpoint

  • Install the sample client dependency.
  • Run a private health check and short request with the recommended starting sampling settings.

    Replace 

    sglang
    with 
    vllm
    for a vLLM deployment. The helper selects a ready worker, opens a temporary port-forward, checks endpoint health, sends the request, and closes the port-forward.

The response resembles the following:

For an authenticated Inference Gateway, use the bearer-token procedure in the HyperPod sample README. Keep credentials out of source code, manifests, and command history.

Measure and tune performance

  • Test each serving path with repeated, representative coding and tool-use requests at the expected concurrency.
  • Record the Beam model version, image digest, instance type, precision, context length, parallelism, serving arguments, cache state, and test repetitions.
  • Measure request success rate, p50 and p95 time to first token, time per output token, end-to-end latency, and aggregate output tokens per second.
  • Tune batch size, KV cache allocation, replica count, autoscaling, and model and image caching from those results.
  • Recheck output quality after changing precision or quantization.

Clean up

Delete resources when you finish testing to avoid ongoing charges.

  • For a SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint, follow the cleanup instructions in the SageMaker JumpStart deployment sample README.
  • For JumpStart, SGLang, or vLLM on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference, follow the cleanup instructions in the HyperPod Inference deployment sample README.
  • Delete a dedicated HyperPod or Amazon EKS cluster created for the walkthrough.
  • Delete unused cached weights, mirrored artifacts, load balancers, log groups, temporary IAM roles, and captured inference data.

Conclusion

Reflection Beam gives developers an open-weight model designed for agentic coding and multi-step tasks. Start with a SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint for a fully managed deployment. Use SageMaker HyperPod Inference with JumpStart when you need Kubernetes-native infrastructure control without managing the serving container, or choose SGLang or vLLM when you need a custom runtime.

Use the SageMaker JumpStart deployment sample or the HyperPod Inference deployment sample, then follow the instructions.

To learn more about Reflection AI and its vision for open intelligence, visit Reflection AI and read Introducing Beam.

entries.title: Meta’s Muse Spark Open now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
entries.summary: Muse Spark Open, Meta's coding-optimized open-weight model, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. Deploy it to a SageMaker AI endpoint in your own AWS account using SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker Python SDK, and run your first inference request.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Meta’s Muse Spark Open now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

Muse Spark Open, Meta’s coding-optimized open-weight model, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, the machine learning (ML) hub of Amazon SageMaker AI. The model was trained on real developer workflows, such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions, and it supports a context window of 1 million tokens. You can deploy it to a SageMaker AI endpoint in your own AWS account in a few steps, without managing the serving infrastructure yourself. SageMaker JumpStart offers two variants: BF16 (

Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B
) and NVFP4 quantized (
Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4
).

In this post, we introduce Muse Spark Open and show you how to deploy the model with Amazon SageMaker Studio and the SageMaker Python SDK, send it a first inference request, and clean up.

Overview of Muse Spark Open

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained for agentic coding workflows, with a focus on first-attempt accuracy, tool calling, and understanding of large codebases. It’s a reasoning model, and it accepts text, images, documents, audio, and audio-video as input and returns text.

Muse Spark Open uses a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture with 816 billion total parameters, of which 42 billion are active for each token. The model holds the capacity of a very large network, while the compute it spends on each token is closer to that of a much smaller dense model. Meta releases the weights under the Muse Model License, which includes the Muse Spark Usage Policy.

The following table summarizes the model.

AttributeMuse Spark Open
ProviderMeta
ArchitectureMixture of experts (MoE), reasoning model
Parameters816B total, 42B active
Context length1M tokens
Input modalitiesText, image, document, audio, audio-video
Output modalitiesText
Variants in SageMaker JumpStartBF16 and NVFP4
LicenseMuse Model License, including the Muse Spark Usage Policy

Built for long-running coding agents

Meta trained Muse Spark Open on the way developers work in real repositories: code generation, debugging, multi-file refactors, and tasks that run for a long time. With the 1 million-token context window, the model can take in a whole project, including its dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files. You don’t need to split a task into smaller pieces to fit the context.

Meta also designed Muse Spark Open as an agentic model from the start. Meta says the model plans, acts, observes the result, and corrects itself over long horizons, rather than making single tool calls. As a reasoning model, it works through a task before it acts, and the SageMaker AI endpoint returns that reasoning alongside the answer, so you can follow what an agent is doing and why. Meta trained the model to browse the web, coordinate subagents for work that can be split up, and operate computers across desktop, mobile, and browser environments. These are capabilities of the model. On SageMaker AI, your application or agent framework provides the tools, browser, and computer-use environment that the model calls. Beyond code, Meta reports that Muse Spark Open reasons across images, documents, audio, and video.

Two properties of the model shape how you serve it. First, sparse activation keeps per-token compute low, but serving still requires enough GPU memory to hold all 816 billion parameters, so the instance choice comes down to memory capacity. Second, the NVFP4 variant stores weights in NVIDIA’s 4-bit floating point format, which needs roughly a quarter of the memory of the BF16 weights. On SageMaker AI, that difference decides the instance: the NVFP4 variant runs on 

ml.p5e.48xlarge
, and the BF16 variant runs on 
ml.p6-b300.48xlarge
. That makes NVFP4 the variant to try first when you size for cost. Evaluate it on your own workloads to confirm the quality fits your use case.

With open weights on SageMaker AI, you also control the deployment. The endpoint runs in your AWS account, so your source code and prompts are processed on infrastructure that you configure and control. You can attach the endpoint to your own Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), encrypt its storage volume with a key from AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS), and turn on network isolation for the container. You also choose the instance type and scaling limits, and you pin the model version, so the model only changes when you redeploy.

Use cases

You can use Muse Spark Open for a wide range of applications. Meta’s focus on coding and agentic workflows suits it to the following use cases:

  • Coding assistants over private repositories: Answer questions about large codebases, refactor them, and debug them with the full project in context, while the code is processed on an endpoint in your account.
  • Long-running coding agents: Run agents that plan a change, edit across multiple files, run tests in your own sandbox, and correct course based on the results.
  • Multimodal engineering workflows: Turn screenshots, design documents, or a recorded bug report with audio and video into a reproduction plan or a draft fix.

Getting started with SageMaker JumpStart

You can deploy Muse Spark Open from SageMaker Studio or with the SageMaker Python SDK. Each path creates a real-time SageMaker AI endpoint in your account.

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure that you have the following:

  • An AWS account with permissions to create SageMaker AI models and endpoints.
  • An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role for SageMaker AI. For this walkthrough, the 
    AmazonSageMakerFullAccess
    managed policy is sufficient. For production, scope the role to the actions and resources that your deployment needs. For details, refer to How to use SageMaker AI execution roles.
  • A SageMaker AI domain with access to SageMaker Studio, for the Studio path. For setup instructions, refer to Use quick setup for Amazon SageMaker AI.
  • Service quota for the endpoint instance type: ml.p5e.48xlarge for endpoint usage for the NVFP4 variant, or ml.p6-b300.48xlarge for endpoint usage for the BF16 variant. To raise a quota, refer to Requesting a quota increase.
  • For the SDK path: Python 3.10 or later and SageMaker Python SDK v3 (
    pip install --upgrade sagemaker
    ).
  • An AWS Region where Muse Spark Open is available in SageMaker JumpStart. At launch, Muse Spark Open is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). To check availability in other Regions, open SageMaker JumpStart in your Region.

The instances that host Muse Spark Open are multi-GPU instances, and you pay for an endpoint for as long as it runs, whether or not it serves requests. Delete the endpoint when you finish, as described in the clean-up section of this post. For rates, refer to Amazon SageMaker AI pricing.

Deploy using SageMaker Studio

The SageMaker Studio path suits a first evaluation: you find the model, review its license, and deploy it from one model detail card.

To find Muse Spark Open in SageMaker JumpStart

  • Open SageMaker Studio.
  • In the navigation pane, choose JumpStart.
  • In the search box, enter Muse Spark Open.
  • Choose Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B for the BF16 variant or Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 for the NVFP4 variant to open its model detail card.

Figure 1 shows the model detail card, which lists the model description, license, and the Deploy option.

To deploy the model

  • On the model detail card, choose Deploy.
  • Muse Spark Open is a gated model, so SageMaker Studio shows its end-user license agreement (EULA). Review the agreement and accept it to continue.
  • For Endpoint name, keep the generated name or enter your own.
  • For Instance type, select ml.p5e.48xlarge for NVFP4 or ml.p6-b300.48xlarge for BF16. SageMaker Studio lists only the instance types that the model supports.
  • For Initial instance count, enter 1.
  • (Optional) Under Advanced options, select a VPC and an AWS KMS key, or turn on network isolation.
  • Choose Deploy.

Figure 2 shows the deployment settings for the NVFP4 variant.

Deployment typically takes 15–20 minutes while SageMaker AI provisions the instance and loads the weights. When the endpoint status changes to InService, the endpoint is ready for requests, as shown in Figure 3.

Deploy using the SageMaker Python SDK

SageMaker JumpStart identifies each variant by a model ID:

  • BF16: 
    meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b
    .
  • NVFP4: 
    meta-vlm-muse-spark-open-816b-a42b-nvfp4
    .

The following code deploys the NVFP4 variant with SageMaker Python SDK v3. You can run it in a SageMaker Studio notebook, which uses your domain’s execution role. In any other Python environment with AWS credentials, pass your SageMaker AI execution role with the 

role_arn
parameter. Muse Spark Open is a gated model, so you must set 
accept_eula=True
to deploy it. To pin a specific model version, add 
model_version
to 
JumpStartConfig
.

Run inference

When the endpoint is in service, send it a request with the 

invoke
method. The endpoint accepts an OpenAI-compatible chat payload with a 
messages
list and returns a chat completion. The final answer is in 
message.content
, the model’s reasoning is in 
message.reasoning_content
, and 
usage.reasoning_tokens
reports how many tokens the reasoning used. Because Muse Spark Open is a reasoning model, leave enough room in 
max_tokens
for its reasoning and the final answer.

The endpoint also supports streaming. To receive tokens as they’re generated, add 

"stream": true
to the request body and call 
endpoint.invoke_with_response_stream
instead of 
invoke
.

Clean up

To stop incurring charges, delete the endpoint when you no longer need it. If you deployed with the SDK, delete the model, the endpoint, and the endpoint configuration:

If you deployed from SageMaker Studio, delete the endpoint in the SageMaker AI console: choose Inference, then Endpoints, select the endpoint, and choose Actions, Delete.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to deploy Muse Spark Open, Meta’s coding-optimized open-weight model, from SageMaker JumpStart to an endpoint in your own AWS account. You used SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker Python SDK and sent the model a first inference request. Benchmark both variants on your own repositories before you choose an instance for production.

To get started, search for Muse Spark Open in SageMaker JumpStart in SageMaker Studio. For more deployment options, such as inference components and optimized deployment configurations, refer to JumpStart foundation model usage in the Amazon SageMaker AI Developer Guide. Before you deploy, review the Muse Model License, which SageMaker JumpStart shows when you deploy the model. For help planning a production deployment, contact AWS.

entries.title: Trust in Depth: Giving agents more autonomy without losing control
entries.summary: Enterprise leaders want AI agents to take on more work but don't fully trust them to act correctly every time. Trust in Depth is AWS's layered approach-scope, know, bound, observe, and prove-that lets agents act on their own when their actions can be verified, reserving human judgment for the decisions that need it.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Trust in Depth: Giving agents more autonomy without losing control

In every conversation I have with enterprise leaders, they say the same thing. They want agents to do more, but they don’t trust them to do it right all the time.

That’s fair. The same creativity and autonomy that makes agents useful makes them hard to trust. Give an agent a task and it finds its own path to finish it, picking tools and sequencing steps no developer scripted. Run the same task twice and it might take a different route each time. A test that passes today tells you little about what the agent does tomorrow.

The usual answer is a person in the loop, approving everything the agent does. That works at small scale, but as agents take on more work, human approvals pile up and review fatigue sets in. People asked to check everything stop catching the things that matter. Caution becomes a bottleneck, and agents capable of far more sit idle on the valuable work that could be making more of an impact.

The fix is to let the agent act on its own when its actions can be verified, and reserve human judgment for the decisions that need it. As agents take on higher stakes work, like financial transactions, a wrong action becomes increasingly harmful. Organizations need the confidence to hand an AI agent important work, knowing it will stay within the limits set, even when no one is watching. That confidence must be built.

Content filtering, testing, and monitoring each serve an important purpose, but none of these capabilities alone can promise an agent will behave correctly the next time it runs. Trust comes from independent layers that reinforce one another, the same layered discipline the industry has practiced for two decades as Defense in Depth, turned to a new purpose. Where Defense in Depth limits what can go wrong, this expands what you can safely allow. AWS calls it Trust in Depth.

Trust in Depth: Trust you can verify

You build trust by answering a set of questions at different moments in the agent’s lifecycle:

  • Scope, before it runs: What is this agent for, what capabilities does the job require, and what must it never do?
  • Know, at deployment: Who authorized it, what identity does it carry, and can you account for every agent acting on your behalf?
  • Bound, while it runs: Do its actions stay within the limits you set, and can it still do the job?
  • Observe, after each run: Can you reconstruct what the agent did and why, and learn from it?

Across these questions, some requirements can be expressed as precise rules, while others call for judgment. A company might require that only a manager can approve access, or that an employee’s sign-in must be blocked before their mailbox can be shared. Other expectations, such as keeping a friendly tone or handling a sensitive situation appropriately, depend on context and human judgment.

For precisely defined rules, testing shows whether the controls work in the cases you anticipate, but an agent takes paths you didn’t. The technology that goes further is automated reasoning, the mathematical logic that checks whether a rule holds in every possible case. It can establish that a rule holds on every path covered by a precise description of the system and its assumptions, or uncover the exact case where it fails. That result is a proof, and it is only as good as the rules and assumptions behind it, which is why the hardest work comes before the agent runs.

AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, from Identity and Access Management (IAM) at more than 2.1 billion requests per second to critical systems like the AWS Nitro Hypervisor, Amazon S3 Block Public Access, and VPC Reachability Analyzer. Now we are bringing it to agents. Wherever an agent’s rules can be stated precisely, automated reasoning can check them.

However, not every rule can be stated precisely. “Only a manager can approve access” can be proven. “Keep a friendly tone” cannot. Where proof does not apply, limit the agent’s access and actions, evaluate its behavior, and send genuine ambiguity to a person to apply judgment. Grant more autonomy as you establish that the relevant rules are enforced, the agent performs reliably on the task, and failures can be detected and handled.

Here is what each Trust in Depth layer asks of you, and how AWS helps you answer it.

Scope your agent to only what the job requires

Trust begins before an agent runs, and this is where to invest the most effort. Problems caught here are cheap to fix. Scoping means deciding what work the agent owns, which tools, data, and services it may reach, the rules it must follow, and which decisions stay with a person.

“Resolve the customer’s issue” says what to achieve, not how the agent may act to achieve it. The agent still needs limits on what it may see, what it may do, and when it must stop and ask. Give it only the access its job requires, and no more. Watch for capabilities no one granted on purpose, the ones bundled with a tool or a role. Grant an admin role for one task, and the agent can inherit permissions across your whole environment.

Scoping starts at the build stage, with how you define the agent. Kiro, the agentic coding system, brings rigor and mature engineering practices to the build stage of agents. It turns high-level intent into structured, spec-driven requirements and uses automated reasoning to surface contradictions, ambiguities, and gaps before any code is written. Kiro also derives property-based tests that check the implementation against those requirements across a wide range of inputs, catching bugs that are hard to detect. Strands provides an open-source tool kit for defining an agent’s model, instructions, and tools, and a managed runtime for operating it. Whatever framework you choose, the responsibility to define the agent’s job and its boundaries is the same.

The next step is turning those boundaries into rules you can hold the agent to. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides governance controls to scale agents safely and governs what the agent does. Using Policies in Bedrock AgentCore, you describe in plain language which tools, APIs, and data the agent may reach, and automated reasoning checks the policy for gaps, like catching a rule that grants too much access, and checks for contradictions that make a rule unable to ever be satisfied, before it takes effect.

Scoping your agent is the hard part, because turning human intent into durable, enforceable policy requires precision and completeness. However, it is also the part that pays off most. Everything that builds on what you set here, and the more precise the policy, the more your agent can safely do on its own.

Know every agent acting on your behalf, and under whose authority

You can’t govern what you can’t see. Teams are creating agents faster than anyone can track them, and an agent no one knows about is an agent no one controls. Every agent needs its own identity, checked every time it acts. No action should be orphaned. When something goes wrong, you can tell which agent did what, and who authorized it.

AWS Agent Registry provides a managed, approved catalog of the agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, tools, and skills across your organization. Administrators use approval workflows to gate what becomes discoverable and remove what no longer meets the bar for security, compliance, and quality. Both people and agents can find and reuse what already exists instead of rebuilding it. But a catalog only tells you what exists. Once the agents are known, AgentCore issues each agent its own identity and checks it on every request, so every action traces back to a specific agent operating under a known authority. That is how you know every agent acting on your behalf.

Bound what your agent says and does, within the limits you set

Setting boundaries matters because an agent can take 10 steps you approved and still reach an outcome no one intended. It can expose sensitive data, drift off topic, or combine permitted actions in ways your policies forbid. Limits can fail in both directions. Too loose, and the agent can do what it shouldn’t. Too tight, and it can’t do its job at all. So let the agent choose how to pursue its task but never rely on it to enforce its own limits. Those limits define the agent’s boundaries and belong in the environment around the agent, enforced deterministically and evaluated across the full sequence of actions, not one step at a time.

This is where the policy you defined in Scope takes effect. Policy in AgentCore enforces it on every tool call routed through AgentCore Gateway, a secure entry point for agents, tools, and models. Because enforcement sits outside the agent’s reasoning, the same checks can hold even when the agent is buggy, manipulated, or hit with a prompt injection: it cannot turn off a control it does not run. Authority does not have to stay fixed either. Because a task’s risk changes as it proceeds, temporal policies weigh what has already happened in a session and adjust permissions as the work continues. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails governs what the agent says and is told. It filters harmful or off-topic content and redacts sensitive data. Automated Reasoning checks go further, proving a response is consistent with the policy you set, not the model’s interpretation of it.

Boundaries also govern what an agent can reach in the first place: which files it can touch, which services it can call, and which credentials it can use. Strands Box, an open-source sandbox, enforces those boundaries from outside the agent’s instructions, so the agent can work with real tools and data but reach only what you allow. The same boundaries hold from a developer’s first local session through to production, so an agent can’t do in production what it couldn’t in development.

Observe what your agent did, then improve it

Even with scoping, identity, and boundaries in place, an agent can respond in milliseconds, with no errors and every dashboard green, and still do the wrong thing. It may have retrieved the wrong information, chosen the wrong tool, or followed a path no one expected. A healthy system is not the same as a successful task. To tell the difference, you must reconstruct what the agent actually did: the context it received, the tools it called, the policy decisions applied, and the result. Testing before deployment remains essential. Production adds evidence about behavior under real conditions and gives operators what they need to investigate, intervene, and improve.

Amazon CloudWatch Omni is built for continual observation. It captures every trace and lays out each step an agent took, from model calls to tool invocations, on a timeline a team can investigate. Its built-in evaluators score agent responses for qualities standard monitoring misses, such as correctness, faithfulness, and whether the agent chose the right tool. And the traces where an agent went wrong become the dataset you test the fix against, so operating an agent and improving it draw on the same evidence.

What Trust in Depth looks like in practice

A manager asks a help desk agent to offboard Sam, an account manager who is leaving the company. The agent needs to remove Sam’s access, transfer his mailbox to his successor, and free up the license the company no longer needs. But Sam’s emails may also contain evidence needed for a client dispute. The wrong sequence could leave Sam with access after he leaves or put that evidence at risk. Security, messaging, legal, and finance each have requirements the agent must follow, even though no one has scripted the full workflow.

Two rules govern the sequence. Sam’s sign-in must be blocked before his mailbox can be converted and shared with his successor. Before changing his email license, the agent must check for a legal hold, a requirement to preserve records for a dispute, and confirm the change keeps those records protected.

Scope. Before the agent runs, the team writes these rules as policies in AgentCore. Each policy requires that the prerequisite step already succeeded for Sam’s account before the next step can run. The agent gets exactly six tools: block sign-in, check for legal holds, place a hold, convert a mailbox, give the successor access, and change a license. It gets no tool to delete the account, because the shared mailbox needs the account to survive.

Know. The agent carries its own identity, so every change to Sam’s account traces back to it.

Bound. The agent tries to convert Sam’s mailbox to a shared one for Priya, the successor. Policy in AgentCore, enforced at the AgentCore Gateway, blocks the call: Sam can still sign in, and converting the mailbox wouldn’t change his password, so his old credentials would still open it. The agent blocks Sam’s sign-in, then converts the mailbox and gives Priya access. Next it moves to the manager’s actual request, freeing up the license, but the gateway blocks that too, because no one has checked Legal’s hold list. The agent checks and finds that Legal requires Sam’s emails to be preserved for a client dispute. It places the hold, confirms it is in effect, then changes Sam’s license to one that supports that protection. The company can reclaim the broader license while keeping the evidence intact.

Observe. Every step is recorded: what the agent tried to do, what the rules decided, the hold, and the outcome.

The agent completed the task without a person approving every step. Its permissions limited what it could change, its identity made those changes traceable, and policies stopped it from acting before the required safeguards were in place. The recorded steps let the team verify that Sam’s access was blocked, his successor could use the mailbox, and the required evidence remained protected.

What becomes possible when agents are trusted

AWS brings these layers together so you can scope an agent to its job, know which agents are acting for you, bound what they do and say, see what they did and improve over time, and prove your rules hold wherever they can be stated precisely. No one layer earns that trust on its own. Together, they are Trust in Depth, and they are what turns a capable agent into an agent that can be trusted to do important work.

You draw the lines: what an agent may do on its own, what needs a person’s approval, and when it must stop. That frees your people for what only people can do: weigh the hard calls, resolve the gray areas, and own the decisions you choose to keep in human hands. As evidence builds that an agent stays inside those lines, you can widen its responsibilities or narrow them.

At AWS, we believe every organization deploying agents, on any platform, should be able to answer these four questions with evidence, and with proof wherever it applies. That is the bar AWS is building for our customers, and the one we invite the industry to hold itself to. Defense in Depth made it safe to connect systems to the world. Trust in Depth makes it safe to let agents act autonomously within it.

Start with one agent, one workflow, and one boundary you can prove. Then expand as the trust is earned.

To begin implementing enforceable rules, explore Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Automated Reasoning checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

entries.title: Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
entries.summary: Learn how to build an agentic intelligent document processing (IDP) system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that classifies, extracts, validates, and learns from business documents with minimal human intervention, automatically handling new document formats without manual template configuration.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

IDC research shows that document-related challenges cost organizations $19,732 for each information worker annually and reduce productivity by 21.3 percent. Organizations receiving invoices from hundreds of suppliers often face layouts that vary by issuer and change without notice. Template-based systems require constant maintenance at this scale. Staff can spend up to 30 percent of their time on document-related tasks, and manual data entry error rates range from 1–4 percent. Conventional intelligent document processing (IDP) solutions address some of this burden, but they require extensive upfront configuration for each document format and break when layouts vary across vendors.

In this post, you learn how to build an agentic IDP system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that classifies, extracts, validates, and learns from business documents with minimal human intervention. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Your agents automatically handle new document formats, such as supplier invoices, purchase orders, insurance claims, and loan applications. By the end of this post, you can:

  • Deploy a multi-agent IDP system, often in under 20 minutes.
  • Process new document types without manual template configuration.
  • Let agents train themselves on each new document format and reuse what they learn, so later documents of that type go straight to extraction without retraining.

Challenges with rule-based document processing

Many IDP pipelines require you to define templates, extraction rules, and validation logic for every document format upfront. When a new vendor sends a purchase order with a different layout, the pipeline breaks. This creates three core challenges:

  • Template rigidity: Each new document format requires manual configuration, and even minor layout changes can cause extraction failures.
  • No learning: The same extraction errors repeat across similar documents because the system doesn’t retain knowledge from previous corrections.
  • Scaling burden: Each new vendor or document variant multiplies the maintenance effort, and organizations processing documents from hundreds of sources face ongoing operational costs.

An agentic approach addresses these challenges. Instead of static templates, AI agents analyze each document, generate extraction instructions, validate results, and learn from corrections automatically. Over time, your system builds a knowledge base of document formats, so you process similar documents with minimal additional configuration.

Solution overview

In this solution, eight specialized agents collaborate across two graph-based workflows running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

The following diagram shows the multi-agent workflow graph built using Strands Agents, an open source SDK for building AI agents.

  • Identification workflow: The Analyzer agent extracts text using Amazon Textract and identifies the document type and sender. The Matcher agent searches for similar documents using vector similarity in Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).
  • Training workflow (new document types): When no match is found, the Instructions agent generates extraction prompts, the Extractor agent extracts structured data, and the Validator agent checks results against schemas and business rules in Amazon Aurora DSQL. If validation fails, the Instructions Fixer agent refines the prompts and retries. On success, the Save Instructions agent persists the instructions for reuse.
  • Automation workflow (known document types): When a match is found, the Extractor agent uses existing instructions. If validation fails, the Troubleshooter agent fixes the extracted data directly without modifying instructions.

How it works

The following diagram shows the infrastructure architecture for the solution.

  • Business documents arrive in Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) or direct upload to Amazon S3.
  • Amazon EventBridge triggers an AWS Lambda function that creates a tracking job in Amazon DynamoDB and invokes AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • AgentCore runtime orchestrates document processing through Strands Agents.
  • Your agents securely access AWS resources through machine-to-machine credentials managed by AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon Cognito.
  • Your Lambda functions become agent-compatible tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface of AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • Agents extract text using Amazon Textract, classify documents using vector embeddings in S3 Vectors, and validate data against business rules in Aurora DSQL.
  • Agents access enterprise data through MCP servers to validate extracted content against business rules.
  • You monitor status and troubleshoot issues through a chat-enabled dashboard hosted on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS).
  • You gain visibility into agent performance through AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon CloudWatch telemetry.

Deploy the solution

Follow these steps to deploy the solution infrastructure and web UI to your AWS account.

Prerequisites

To deploy this solution, you must have:

  • An AWS account.
  • Access to Amazon Bedrock with Amazon Nova and Anthropic (Claude) models enabled. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
  • Access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Runtime, Gateway, Identity), S3 Vectors, and Amazon Aurora DSQL in a supported Region.
  • AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) v2 installed.
  • Docker installed and running (required for building and deploying container images).
  • Python 3.11+ and Node.js 18+.
  • AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to create S3 buckets, Lambda functions, DynamoDB tables, Cognito user pools, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories, and Amazon ECS services.
  • Clone the repository and set up the environment:
  • Deploy the stacks:

This deploys six AWS CloudFormation stacks: Core (S3, Cognito, DynamoDB), Gateway (Lambda tools, AgentCore Gateway), Aurora (Amazon Aurora DSQL), Agent (AgentCore runtime, containers), UI Orchestrator (API endpoints), and Modern UI (React app on Amazon CloudFront). Deployment takes approximately 15–20 minutes.

  • Verify deployment by checking that each stack shows 
    CREATE_COMPLETE
    in the CloudFormation console.

Process files and review results

After deployment, you receive an email with the CloudFront URL, username, and temporary password.

Process a document

  • Sign in to the web UI and choose Process Document.
  • Upload a sample purchase order from 
    infrastructure/sample_data/purchase_orders/training/
    .
  • The document enters the agent workflow:
    • The Analyzer agent extracts text and identifies the sender and document type.
    • The Matcher agent searches for similar documents in the vector store.
    • For a new document type, the training workflow generates extraction instructions, extracts data, validates it, and saves the instructions for future use.
    • For a known document type, the automation workflow extracts data using existing instructions and validates it.
  • Review results in the Review Jobs and Instructions tab to verify extracted data, validation results, and generated instructions.

Example: A new document type (training workflow)

Suppose you upload the first purchase order from a new retailer, Two Wheel Store. The Matcher agent searches the vector store, finds no similar document, and routes the job through the training workflow.

The Analyzer agent uses Amazon Textract to extract the raw document text:

The Instructions agent generates extraction prompts from the schema, and the Extractor agent produces structured JSON:

The Validator agent checks the result against the schema and fails:

The vendor’s SKU format (

SB-004
) doesn’t match Acme Bikes’ internal format (
AB-SB-004
). The Instructions Fixer agent diagnoses the mismatch and adds an explicit SKU transformation rule to the extraction prompt: prefix vendor SKUs with 
AB-
. On the second pass, the seven line items validate successfully, and the Save Instructions agent persists the refined prompt to the vector store. End-to-end time for this first run: 3 minutes 49 seconds.

Example: A known document type (automation workflow)

When a second purchase order from Two Wheel Store arrives, the Matcher agent finds the stored instructions from the first run with a confidence score of 3.946 (threshold: 3.7) and routes the job through the automation workflow:

  • The Extractor agent applies the stored instructions directly, so the orchestrator skips prompt generation. The SKU transformation rule learned during training applies automatically (
    EL-002
    → 
    AB-EL-002
    , 
    HB-071
    → 
    AB-HB-071
    , 
    PD-002
    → 
    AB-PD-002
    ).
  • The three line items validate on the first pass with an order total of $5,979.19.
  • End-to-end processing completes in 1 minute 30 seconds, down from 3 minutes 49 seconds on the first run.

Use the interactive chat

The dashboard includes a chat interface for troubleshooting:

  • Ask 
    what tools do you have
    to see available agent capabilities.
  • Ask 
    list instructions
    to view stored extraction instructions.
  • Ask 
    what is the status of job XXXX
    to check processing progress.
  • Ask 
    what went wrong with job XXXX, how can we update the instructions?
    to diagnose failures.

Understand how accuracy improves over time

The system improves over time through two feedback loops:

  • Training loop: When the Instructions Fixer agent refines extraction prompts after validation failures, the improved instructions are saved and reused for similar documents.
  • Processing loop: When the Troubleshooter agent fixes extraction errors, it provides detailed analysis that helps identify patterns in document format variations.

When changing models, use AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to confirm that extraction quality remains acceptable. The solution already uses AgentCore Observability, so it has the required instrumentation.

Estimated cost

You pay only for what you use, because the solution runs on serverless and on-demand resources with no idle costs. For a workload of 10 training documents and 1,000 processed documents each month in US East (N. Virginia), the estimated cost is approximately $58 per month. Foundation model (FM) inference through Amazon Bedrock represents approximately 85 percent of the total cost, at roughly $0.055 per document. Actual cost depends largely on the models assigned to each agent. Model choices are centralized in 

agents/orchestratorgraph/utils/config.py
, so you can use lower-cost models for simpler tasks and stronger models where needed. For detailed pricing, refer to the Amazon Bedrock pricing page.

Customize the solution for your use case

You get a purchase order processing use case with a synthetic bike company dataset, a pre-built JSON schema, and a validation Lambda function that checks extracted data against product and vendor records in a mock ERP database. To process your own documents, you must replace the included schemas and validation logic with your own.

Define your document schema

Create a JSON schema that defines the fields you want to extract for each document type. The sample purchase order schema in 

agents/orchestratorgraph/doc_schema/purchase_order_schema.json
provides a reference. Your schema should specify field names, data types, and whether each field is explicitly stated in the document or inferred from context.

Build your validation process

The included validator checks purchase order data against synthetic vendor and product tables in Aurora DSQL. Your production implementation requires a validation process tailored to your business rules. For example:

  • An invoice validator might check vendor IDs against your accounts payable system and verify line item totals match the invoice total.
  • A contract validator might verify that the document contains required clauses and that dates and party names match your records.
  • A claims validator might check policy numbers, coverage limits, and claimant information against your policy management system.

To add a new validator, create a Lambda function that accepts extracted JSON and returns a pass/fail result with detailed error messages, then register it as a tool in AgentCore Gateway. Refer to 

gateway/tools/po_validator_tool/
for the implementation pattern.

Update agent prompts

The agent prompts in 

agents/orchestratorgraph/prompts/
reference purchase order terminology. Update these prompts to reflect your document types and extraction requirements. The Orchestrator agent, Validator agent, and Instructions agent each contain document-type-specific language that you should adapt.

Best practices

Keep these recommendations in mind as you train and operate your agentic IDP system.

  • Start with representative samples: Upload 5–10 documents per type during training, including edge cases with format variations, to build reliable extraction instructions.
  • Use business rule validation: Connect validators to your reference data (vendor lists, product catalogs) in Aurora DSQL to catch extraction errors early.
  • Monitor agent performance: Use AgentCore Observability and CloudWatch to track execution paths, identify bottlenecks, and measure extraction accuracy over time.
  • Add document types incrementally: Create a JSON schema for each new document type and a corresponding validation Lambda function. The agents handle the rest.
  • Add guardrails for production: Apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content filtering and grounding checks on agent outputs. This is especially important when you process sensitive document types such as insurance claims or loan applications.
  • Review the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs: Consult the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs and Generative AI Apps for security considerations when building applications that use large language models (LLMs).

Clean up

Important: Before running cleanup, export the data you want to retain. The 

destroy.py
script permanently deletes processed documents (S3), job history (DynamoDB), validation data (Aurora DSQL), and learned extraction instructions (vector store).

To avoid ongoing charges, remove the deployed resources:

Verify that the six CloudFormation stacks are deleted on the console: AgenticIDP-Core-Dev, AgenticIDP-Gateway-Dev, AgenticIDP-Aurora-Dev, AgenticIDP-Agent-Dev, AgenticIDP-UIOrchestr-Dev, and AgenticIDP-ModernUI-Dev.

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to build a self-improving document processing system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, where specialized AI agents collaborate to classify, extract, validate, and learn from business documents. This agentic approach adapts to new document formats automatically and improves accuracy over time through feedback loops, replacing manual template configuration with autonomous learning.

As next steps:

  • Deploy the sample solution and test with the included purchase order samples.
  • Add your own document types by creating JSON schemas and validation rules.
  • Explore how to integrate extracted data with downstream systems such as ERP, CRM, or content management tools.

To learn more about the services and patterns used in this post, refer to the following resources:

  • For a deep dive into the agent framework used in this solution, refer to Strands Agents SDK: A technical deep dive into agent architectures and observability.
  • To understand how AgentCore Gateway transforms APIs into agent-compatible tools, refer to Introducing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: Transforming enterprise AI agent tool development.
  • For background on the Model Context Protocol and how it integrates with AWS services, refer to Unlocking the power of Model Context Protocol (MCP) on AWS.
  • To learn how agents can retain context across sessions, refer to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory: Building context-aware agents.
  • For details on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capabilities, refer to the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation.

For expert guidance on building document processing solutions, AWS Professional Services and AWS Partners can help.

entries.title: Generate presentations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
entries.summary: This post walks you through building an AI agent system with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates PowerPoint presentation creation from enterprise documents. A supervisor agent, Retrieval Augmented Generation, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails generate grounded presentations in under 90 seconds.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Generate presentations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

A financial services team spends significant time each week manually creating client PowerPoint presentations from quarterly reports, compliance documents, and market analyses. Each presentation requires reading hundreds of pages, extracting key data points, structuring slides, and generating supporting visuals. This post walks you through building an AI agent system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates this workflow, completing in under 90 seconds in our internal testing. This approach reduces presentation creation time while grounding content in source documents. The solution deploys a supervisor agent on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using the Strands Agents framework to orchestrate document generation and summarization tools. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (available on Amazon Bedrock) handles content creation, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 powers vector search, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available on Amazon Bedrock) generates slide images. This post includes a public repository with the code assets.

Solution overview

The solution deploys a single supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime that selects between document generation and summarization tools based on user requests. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline uses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector storage and semantic search across multimodal content.

The solution includes a REST API built with .NET 8 minimal APIs, so you can integrate with existing enterprise applications through standard HTTP calls. AWS Lambda offers serverless compute, including containerized functions for PowerPoint generation. The solution secures the implementation with Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) isolation, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) least-privilege access control.

Key concepts

This section covers AgentCore runtime, RAG, and content safety guardrails as they apply to this solution.

Agent orchestration with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

A single AI agent generating documents from large knowledge bases must retrieve content, structure outlines, generate text, create images, and assemble files. Rather than implementing these competing responsibilities in a monolithic function, the solution uses a tool-based architecture where a supervisor agent routes requests to specialized tools.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent code runs in an isolated container with session management, built-in identity, and observability. The solution uses the Strands Agents framework (an open source SDK for building AI agents) to implement the supervisor logic.

The supervisor agent exposes two tools:

  • generate_pptx: Creates PowerPoint presentations by invoking the PPTX Generator Lambda function, which retrieves content from the knowledge base, generates slide outlines, creates AI images, and assembles the final document.
  • generate_summary: Extracts and synthesizes information from the knowledge base using RAG to deliver accurate, grounded responses.

The agent determines whether a request requires document generation, content summarization, or both, then invokes the appropriate tool. You can add new capabilities by defining new tools in the agent code without modifying existing ones.

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) for enterprise knowledge

RAG addresses a fundamental challenge in AI systems: delivering accurate, up-to-date information grounded in enterprise data rather than relying solely on the model’s training data. The implementation uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, which combine vector search with large language models (LLMs) to retrieve relevant context before generating responses.

The RAG pipeline works as follows:

  • You upload enterprise documents to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).
  • The system chunks and parses documents, applying special handling for multimodal content including tables, charts, and images.
  • Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 converts each chunk into high-dimensional vectors that capture semantic meaning.
  • Amazon OpenSearch Serverless stores the vectors, creating a searchable vector database.
  • At query time, the system converts the user’s request into an embedding and performs similarity search to retrieve relevant document chunks.
  • Retrieved chunks supply context to the language model, which generates responses grounded in the source material.

This approach is designed to help reduce hallucinated content by grounding generated documents in source information from the enterprise knowledge base.

Note: The Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection data plane must remain publicly accessible because Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases accesses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless from AWS-managed infrastructure, not through customer VPC endpoints. IAM data access policies protect the collection, and VPC-only access restricts the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless dashboard.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content safety

Enterprise AI applications require content moderation to meet organizational standards and compliance requirements. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails offers built-in content filtering and safety mechanisms integrated throughout the document generation pipeline.

Guardrails operate at multiple stages:

  • Input processing: Filters user requests to help prevent injection issues and inappropriate content.
  • Output generation: Monitors model outputs to verify compliance with content policies.
  • Personally identifiable information (PII) handling: Detects and anonymizes or blocks PII.

The implementation creates custom guardrails through AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), configured with specific policies tailored to enterprise document creation. The agent applies guardrails at the model invocation level, providing consistent content safety without requiring manual configuration for each deployment.

Solution architecture

The following diagram illustrates the agent-based document generation system.

The data flow begins with user requests arriving through Amazon API Gateway, which routes them to a .NET-based Chat API running on AWS Lambda. The API maintains conversation state in Amazon DynamoDB. It then invokes the supervisor agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime.

The supervisor agent analyzes the request and selects the appropriate tool. For document generation, it invokes the PPTX Generator Lambda (a containerized Python function). For summarization, the supervisor invokes the Summary Generator Lambda, which queries the knowledge base through the 

retrieve_and_generate
API.

The system processes, chunks, and embeds documents stored in Amazon S3 using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless indexes the embeddings for fast semantic search. When tools query the knowledge base, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless retrieves relevant chunks, which are then supplied as context to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (on Amazon Bedrock) for generating grounded responses.

The system stores generated documents in Amazon S3 and returns presigned URLs for secure download. Security measures include:

  • AWS WAF with managed rule sets and IP-based rate limiting on Amazon API Gateway.
  • Amazon Cognito with the Plus feature plan and advanced security mode for threat protection.
  • Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provisioned through AWS CDK for consistent content filtering.
  • Amazon DynamoDB with point-in-time recovery, deletion protection, and customer-managed AWS KMS encryption.
  • Amazon S3 buckets with versioning, server access logging, and block public access.
  • AWS X-Ray tracing on Lambda functions for distributed debugging.
  • Input validation with regex-based tenant ID and session ID verification.
  • Tenant isolation through AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) role assumption per tenant.

Prerequisites

Before deploying, you need the following tools and access configured in your environment:

  • AWS environment:
    • An active AWS account with permissions for deploying infrastructure.
    • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with credentials.
    • IAM role with appropriate service access policies.
  • Development tools:
    • .NET SDK 8 with Amazon.Lambda.Tools installed globally.
    • Python 3.12 or later for AWS CDK and Lambda functions.
    • Node.js and AWS CDK CLI for infrastructure deployment.
    • Docker or Finch for building container images (ARM64 support required).
  • AWS services access:
    • Amazon Bedrock with model access for Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available through Amazon Bedrock). For model availability by Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
    • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore access enabled in your account.
    • Amazon API Gateway Regional REST API integration timeout configured to at least 300 seconds. The default is 29 seconds. For more information, see API Gateway quotas.
    • An existing Amazon VPC with private subnets.
    • An Amazon S3 bucket for deployment artifacts.

Set up the solution

The setup process includes configuring deployment parameters and initializing the AWS CDK environment.

  • Clone the repository and navigate to the project directory:
  • Create the configuration file 
    pipeline-params.ini
    at the repository root:

    Set 

    awscliprofile
    to your AWS CLI profile name, or leave empty to use environment variable credentials.
  • Bootstrap AWS CDK (one-time per account and Region):

    This creates the AWS CloudFormation CDKToolkit stack required for AWS CDK deployments.

  • Make build scripts executable:

Build and deploy

The deployment consists of three phases: building artifacts, deploying infrastructure, and deploying the AgentCore runtime agent.

Build phase

The build phase compiles application code and packages deployment artifacts. Run the build script:

This compiles the .NET projects (Chat API) and packages them as Lambda deployment packages. It builds the PPTX Generator container image using Docker or Finch and authenticates with Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). It then pushes the container image and stores build artifacts in the 

asset-output
directory.

Infrastructure deployment phase

The infrastructure deployment creates AWS resources and configures service integrations. Run the deployment script:

The deployment creates four AWS CloudFormation stacks in dependency order:

  • VPCEndpointsStack: Configures Amazon VPC endpoints for AWS services including Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • OpensearchStack: Provisions Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection for vector storage.
  • AgentCoreStack: Creates guardrails, Lambda functions, IAM roles, and stores configuration in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store.
  • ChatApiStack: Deploys Amazon API Gateway and Chat API Lambda.

AgentCore runtime deployment

After the infrastructure stacks are deployed, deploy the supervisor agent to AgentCore runtime:

This script builds the supervisor agent container (ARM64), pushes it to Amazon ECR, creates the AgentCore runtime and endpoint, and updates the Systems Manager parameter with the endpoint Amazon Resource Name (ARN). The Chat API references this endpoint ARN to route requests to the agent.

After deployment, AWS CloudFormation outputs include the Amazon API Gateway endpoint URL and resource identifiers.

Configuration

The solution offers several configuration points:

Agent instructions

Edit 

agent/app.py
to modify the supervisor agent’s system prompt and behavior. The agent uses Strands Agents with two tools defined in 
agent/tools.py
:
  • generate_pptx: Invokes the PPTX Generator Lambda for document creation.
  • generate_summary: Invokes the Summary Generator Lambda for knowledge base queries.

Model selection

In 

pipeline-params.ini
, adjust model identifiers:
  • ParsingInferenceProfileId
    : Model for knowledge base document parsing (Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5 recommended for cost efficiency).
  • AgentInferenceProfileId
    : Model for agent reasoning (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 recommended).
  • EmbeddingModelId
    : Embedding model for vector search (Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2).
  • ImageGenerationModelId
    : Model for slide image generation (Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint).

With inference profiles instead of direct model IDs, requests draw on a broader multi-Region capacity pool, which increases throughput and helps maintain consistent performance under load.

Lambda configuration

Adjust compute resources in the stack files:

  • Chat API: 128 MB memory, 29-second timeout, 100 reserved concurrency (in 
    api.py
    ).
  • PPTX Generator: 900 MB memory, 300-second timeout, 50 reserved concurrency (in 
    pptx_gen.py
    ).
  • Summary Generator: 512 MB memory, 300-second timeout, 50 reserved concurrency (in 
    sum_gen.py
    ).

Results

In internal testing with a 90-page Amazon 2024 Annual Report PDF, the solution produced the following performance metrics:

  • Presentation generation time: 70–90 seconds end-to-end (including knowledge base retrieval, content generation, image creation, and file assembly).
  • Slide count: Six slides with title, bullet points, image+text, image-only, and takeaway formats.
  • Image generation: Two AI-generated images per presentation using Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint.
  • Cost per generation: Approximately $0.04 in model invocation costs at time of writing in us-east-1 (text and image generation, with image generation accounting for the majority of cost).
  • Knowledge base ingestion: Under 2 minutes for a single 1.3 MB PDF document.

PowerPoint presentations

The following figures show example slides from a generated presentation.

Generated presentations include:

  • Title slides with customizable branding.
  • Content slides with bullet points and structured text.
  • Image slides with AI-generated visuals from Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (on Amazon Bedrock).
  • Speaker notes with presentation guidance.
  • Consistent formatting based on corporate templates.

Summaries

Summary outputs provided to the knowledge base include:

  • Concise synthesis of knowledge base content.
  • Citation tracking to source documents.
  • Structured formatting with key points highlighted.

API responses

The Chat API returns:

  • Streaming responses for real-time user feedback. Because internal testing showed that presentation generation takes 70–90 seconds (exceeding the default Amazon API Gateway 29-second integration timeout), the Chat API uses an asynchronous invocation pattern. Use streaming or polling to receive the final result rather than waiting on a synchronous REST call.
  • Conversation context maintenance across multiple turns.
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs for document downloads (5-minute expiration).

Generated content undergoes Amazon Bedrock Guardrails validation to verify compliance with content policies before delivery.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the deployed resources:

  • Delete the AgentCore runtime and endpoint:
  • Turn off Amazon DynamoDB deletion protection (required before stack deletion):
  • Delete AWS CloudFormation stacks in reverse dependency order:
  • Empty Amazon S3 buckets before deletion (AWS CloudFormation cannot delete non-empty buckets):
  • Delete Amazon ECR repositories containing container images:
  • Delete tenant knowledge base sub-stacks (created by the tenant provisioner):

Security considerations

This solution uses Lambda environment variables for configuration values such as model IDs, Amazon S3 bucket names, and guardrail IDs. These are resource identifiers, not secrets. For production deployments, use AWS Secrets Manager for sensitive configuration values such as API keys and database credentials.

The AgentCore runtime agent runs in an isolated container with session-level isolation. Each user session operates in a dedicated environment, helping to prevent cross-session data contamination.

Conclusion

In this post, you built an AI agent system with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates enterprise document generation. The supervisor agent deployed on AgentCore runtime routes requests to specialized tools for document creation and summarization, reducing presentation creation to about 90 seconds in an internal test.

The RAG pipeline grounds generated content in source documents, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails verifies content compliance. You can adapt this architecture for automated report generation in financial services, technical documentation for engineering teams, or proposal creation for sales organizations.

To get started, clone the GitHub repository and follow the setup instructions. For more information about the services used, refer to the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation, Strands Agents SDK, and AWS CDK Developer Guide.

entries.title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
entries.summary: Learn how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock that autonomously investigates and safely remediates cloud security findings from CNAPP and cloud-native sources. The approach drove a 90%+ reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock

Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount.

In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock, to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues.

About Tamnoon

Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers.

Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale.

Cloud security remediation challenges

A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts.

  • Alert volume overwhelms headcount: CNAPPs and scanners generate thousands of findings. Teams can’t triage them all, so critical exposures sit unresolved while risk compounds for months.
  • Investigation is manual and repetitive: Each finding requires context gathering on who owns the resource, what depends on it, whether the fix is safe. This eats hours of senior engineer time, repeated across every item in the backlog.
  • Fear of production impact blocks automation: Teams hesitate to automate remediation because they can’t risk taking down production. Without confidence that a fix is safe, nothing moves.
  • Reactive prioritization: Without a way to cluster related findings or score remediation confidence, teams work through alerts linearly rather than addressing root causes that resolve many issues at once.

Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems.

Solution overview

Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely.

Agentic architecture on Amazon Bedrock

The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline:
